claim: ApoE ε4 genotype is the strongest and most prevalent risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) ε4 genotype is the strongest and most prevalent risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Corder et al., 1993; Schmechel et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corder et al., 1993 and Schmechel et al., 1993.

claim: ApoE binds to and modulates the function of ApoE receptors, a family of LDL receptor-related proteins (LRPs).
source: ApoE binds to and modulates the function of ApoE receptors, a family of LDL receptor-related proteins (LRPs) and postsynaptic signal transducers that regulate glutamatergic neurotransmission in the CNS (Weeber et al., 2002; Beffert et al., 2005; Herz and Chen, 2006) and the formation of the neuromuscular synapse in the periphery (Weatherbee et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Weeber et al., 2002; Beffert et al., 2005; Herz and Chen, 2006.

claim: ApoE receptors regulate glutamatergic neurotransmission in the CNS.
source: ApoE binds to and modulates the function of ApoE receptors, a family of LDL receptor-related proteins (LRPs) and postsynaptic signal transducers that regulate glutamatergic neurotransmission in the CNS (Weeber et al., 2002; Beffert et al., 2005; Herz and Chen, 2006) and the formation of the neuromuscular synapse in the periphery (Weatherbee et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weeber et al., 2002; Beffert et al., 2005; Herz and Chen, 2006.

claim: ApoE receptors regulate the formation of the neuromuscular synapse in the periphery.
source: ApoE binds to and modulates the function of ApoE receptors, a family of LDL receptor-related proteins (LRPs) and postsynaptic signal transducers that regulate glutamatergic neurotransmission in the CNS (Weeber et al., 2002; Beffert et al., 2005; Herz and Chen, 2006) and the formation of the neuromuscular synapse in the periphery (Weatherbee et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weatherbee et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2008b.

claim: Mutations in the amyloid precursor protein (APP) cause early-onset AD.
source: Mutations in the amyloid precursor protein (APP) cause early-onset AD (Goate et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Goate et al., 1991.

claim: APP and its pathogenic cleavage product, β-amyloid, physically and functionally interact with ApoE receptors on multiple levels.
source: APP and its pathogenic cleavage product, β-amyloid, physically and functionally interact with ApoE receptors on multiple levels (Kounnas et al., 1995), by regulating the trafficking and processing of APP (Ulery et al., 2000; Pietrzik et al., 2002; Andersen et al., 2005; Hoe et al., 2005; Pietrzik and Jaeger, 2008; Marzolo and Bu, 2009), mediating amyloid clearance (Andersen et al., 2005; Deane et al., 2008) and by preventing amyloid-induced synaptic suppression at the synapse (Durakoglugil et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Kounnas et al., 1995; Ulery et al., 2000; Pietrzik et al., 2002; and others.

claim: APP is expressed at the neuromuscular junction.
source: Intriguingly, APP is also expressed at the neuromuscular junction (Akaaboune et al., 2000) and APP family members are required for normal formation and function of the neuromuscular junction (Torroja et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2005, 2009), although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Akaaboune et al., 2000.

claim: APP family members are required for normal formation and function of the neuromuscular junction.
source: Intriguingly, APP is also expressed at the neuromuscular junction (Akaaboune et al., 2000) and APP family members are required for normal formation and function of the neuromuscular junction (Torroja et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2005, 2009), although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Torroja et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2005, 2009.

claim: APP family members contribute to synaptic function in the CNS.
source: APP family members have also been shown to contribute to synaptic function in the CNS (Weyer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weyer et al., 2011.

claim: ApoE ε4 genotype strongly predisposes to an earlier age of AD onset, increasing the relative risk in individuals >65 years of age by approximately 10-fold.
source: ApoE ε4 genotype strongly predisposes to an earlier age of AD onset, increasing the relative risk in individuals >65 years of age by approximately 10-fold (Corder et al., 1993; Schmechel et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corder et al., 1993; Schmechel et al., 1993.

claim: APP and ApoE interact with LRPs.
source: APP and ApoE interact with LRPs, thus suggesting a role of ApoE receptors in AD pathogenesis (Herz and Beffert, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herz and Beffert, 2000.

claim: ApoE receptors serve as cargo receptors that can mediate the endocytosis of ApoE containing lipoprotein particles.
source: Besides serving as cargo receptors that can mediate the endocytosis of ApoE containing lipoprotein particles, ApoE receptors have also been shown to function as signal transducers that regulate essential signaling pathways during development and in the adult organism, where they control glutamate receptor function, synaptic plasticity, memory and learning (reviewed in Herz and Chen, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herz and Chen, 2006.

claim: ApoE receptors function as signal transducers that regulate essential signaling pathways during development and in the adult organism.
source: Besides serving as cargo receptors that can mediate the endocytosis of ApoE containing lipoprotein particles, ApoE receptors have also been shown to function as signal transducers that regulate essential signaling pathways during development and in the adult organism, where they control glutamate receptor function, synaptic plasticity, memory and learning (reviewed in Herz and Chen, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herz and Chen, 2006.

claim: ApoE receptors control glutamate receptor function, synaptic plasticity, memory and learning.
source: Besides serving as cargo receptors that can mediate the endocytosis of ApoE containing lipoprotein particles, ApoE receptors have also been shown to function as signal transducers that regulate essential signaling pathways during development and in the adult organism, where they control glutamate receptor function, synaptic plasticity, memory and learning (reviewed in Herz and Chen, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herz and Chen, 2006.

claim: Both APP and LRP4 are required for normal NMJ formation.
source: Both APP and LRP4 are required for normal NMJ formation, and the LRP4 ligand agrin is abundantly expressed in the CNS (Burgess et al., 2000; O'Connor et al., 1994; Stone and Nikolics, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2000; O'Connor et al., 1994; Stone and Nikolics, 1995.

claim: The LRP4 ligand agrin is abundantly expressed in the CNS.
source: Both APP and LRP4 are required for normal NMJ formation, and the LRP4 ligand agrin is abundantly expressed in the CNS (Burgess et al., 2000; O'Connor et al., 1994; Stone and Nikolics, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2000; O'Connor et al., 1994; Stone and Nikolics, 1995.

claim: MuSK localizes to excitatory synapses.
source: Furthermore, MuSK localizes to excitatory synapses (Ksiazek et al., 2007) and has been shown to mediate cholinergic responses, synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Garcia-Osta et al., 2006), while agrin was found to regulate synaptogenesis (McCroskery et al., 2009) and prevent synapse loss in the cortex (Ksiazek et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ksiazek et al., 2007.

claim: MuSK mediates cholinergic responses, synaptic plasticity and memory formation.
source: Furthermore, MuSK localizes to excitatory synapses (Ksiazek et al., 2007) and has been shown to mediate cholinergic responses, synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Garcia-Osta et al., 2006), while agrin was found to regulate synaptogenesis (McCroskery et al., 2009) and prevent synapse loss in the cortex (Ksiazek et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Garcia-Osta et al., 2006.

claim: Agrin regulates synaptogenesis.
source: Furthermore, MuSK localizes to excitatory synapses (Ksiazek et al., 2007) and has been shown to mediate cholinergic responses, synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Garcia-Osta et al., 2006), while agrin was found to regulate synaptogenesis (McCroskery et al., 2009) and prevent synapse loss in the cortex (Ksiazek et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McCroskery et al., 2009.

claim: Agrin prevents synapse loss in the cortex.
source: Furthermore, MuSK localizes to excitatory synapses (Ksiazek et al., 2007) and has been shown to mediate cholinergic responses, synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Garcia-Osta et al., 2006), while agrin was found to regulate synaptogenesis (McCroskery et al., 2009) and prevent synapse loss in the cortex (Ksiazek et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ksiazek et al., 2007.

claim: LRP4 and APP physically bind to each other.
source: We found that LRP4 and APP physically bind to each other and that APP can also bind agrin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 6A).

claim: APP can bind agrin.
source: We found that LRP4 and APP physically bind to each other and that APP can also bind agrin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 8B).

claim: Ligation of LRP4 by immobilized APP can activate MuSK in the absence of neural agrin.
source: Ligation of LRP4 by immobilized APP can activate MuSK in the absence of neural agrin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 7C).

claim: Simultaneous and stoichiometric interaction of APP, LRP4, and agrin favors the formation of a hetero-oligomeric complex.
source: Simultaneous and stoichiometric interaction of the three proteins favors the formation of a hetero-oligomeric complex, which may serve to focus the formation of the NMJ at the surface of the myotube.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing cooperative binding (Figure 8C) and inference from the results.

claim: Mice carrying a novel Lrp4 null allele die perinatally from a complete failure to form NMJs.
source: Consistent with the previous report that mice with point mutations in Lrp4 die at birth (Weatherbee et al., 2006), mice carrying a novel Lrp4 null allele, which we generated by deleting exon 1 of murine Lrp4 (Figure 1A), also die perinatally from a complete failure to form NMJs (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Weatherbee et al., 2006.

claim: Mice carrying an Lrp4 allele encoding a truncated receptor consisting of only the extracellular domain (ECD), but lacking the transmembrane segment and intracellular domain (ICD), are viable.
source: By contrast, mice carrying an Lrp4 allele encoding a truncated receptor consisting of only the extracellular domain (ECD), but lacking the transmembrane segment and intracellular domain (ICD), are viable (Johnson et al., 2005), indicating that at least partially functional NMJs must form and that thus neither membrane anchoring of the LRP4 ECD nor its ICD is absolutely required for the formation of the NMJ (Dietrich et al., 2010; Gomez and Burden, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2005.

claim: Neither membrane anchoring of the LRP4 ECD nor its ICD is absolutely required for the formation of the NMJ.
source: By contrast, mice carrying an Lrp4 allele encoding a truncated receptor consisting of only the extracellular domain (ECD), but lacking the transmembrane segment and intracellular domain (ICD), are viable (Johnson et al., 2005), indicating that at least partially functional NMJs must form and that thus neither membrane anchoring of the LRP4 ECD nor its ICD is absolutely required for the formation of the NMJ (Dietrich et al., 2010; Gomez and Burden, 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the viability of Lrp4ECD/ECD mice and supported by citations to Dietrich et al., 2010; Gomez and Burden, 2011.

claim: In Lrp4ECD/ECD mice, neuromuscular synapses were present in the E16.5 embryos.
source: In contrast to the complete absence of pre- and postsynaptic differentiation in Lrp4 null mice (Figure 2A, middle row), neuromuscular synapses were present in the E16.5 Lrp4ECD/ECD embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Presynaptic terminals were properly juxtaposed to postsynaptic AChR clusters in E16.5 Lrp4ECD/ECD embryos.
source: Presynaptic terminals were properly juxtaposed to postsynaptic AChR clusters (Figure 2A, bottom row), which aligned along the central region of the muscle, although the density of the AChR appeared reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NMJs developed normally in the Lrp4ΔICD/ΔICD mice.
source: NMJs developed normally in the Lrp4ΔICD/ΔICD mice (Figure 2B, middle column), with synapse size indistinguishable from wild type (left column).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The impaired development of NMJs in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice continues during the postnatal period.
source: By contrast, the impaired development of NMJs in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice continues during the postnatal period.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 3A.

claim: AChR clusters were distributed more diffusely in P12 triangularis sterni muscle of Lrp4ECD/ECD mice, compared with wild-type or Lrp4ΔICD/ΔICD mice.
source: AChR clusters were distributed more diffusely in P12, the triangularis sterni muscle of Lrp4ECD/ECD mice, compared with wild-type or Lrp4ΔICD/ΔICD mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In adult muscles, the NMJ from Lrp4ECD/ECD mice remained noticeably smaller than that from age-matched wild-type mice.
source: In adult muscles, the NMJ from Lrp4ECD/ECD mice remained noticeably smaller than that from age-matched wild-type mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the triangularis sterni muscle from 3-month old Lrp4ECD/ECD mice, the pre-synaptic nerve terminal and post-synaptic AChR clusters remained markedly smaller compared with wild type.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, in the triangularis sterni muscle from 3-month old Lrp4ECD/ECD mice, the pre-synaptic nerve terminal and post-synaptic AChR clusters remained markedly smaller compared with wild type.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The NMJ in Lrp4ΔICD/ΔICD mice developed to similar size as wild type.
source: By contrast, the NMJ in Lrp4ΔICD/ΔICD mice developed to similar size as wild type (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LRP4 membrane anchoring is required for the growth and maturation of the NMJ.
source: Thus, although the NMJ was established in Lrp4ECD/ECD embryos, it remained considerably smaller (compared with age-matched wild-type control) at postnatal and adult stages, indicating that LRP4 membrane anchoring is required for the growth and maturation of the NMJ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing smaller NMJs in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice at postnatal and adult stages.

claim: The ultrastructure of the nerve terminal and post-synaptic membrane appeared largely normal in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice—with abundant presynaptic vesicles and elaborate junctional folds.
source: Intriguingly, the ultrastructure of the nerve terminal and post-synaptic membrane appeared largely normal—with abundant presynaptic vesicles and elaborate junctional folds (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only a minor fraction (2%) of synapses was innervated by more than one axon in Lrp4ECD/ECD NMJs at P12.
source: Furthermore, despite a significant reduction in sizes, only a minor fraction (2%) of synapses was innervated by more than one axon in Lrp4ECD/ECD NMJs at P12, as was the case in the wild type.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: The γ-ε switch occurred normally in the Lrp4ECD/ECD mutant.
source: Moreover, the γ-ε switch also occurred normally in the Lrp4ECD/ECD mutant. By P16 γ-AChR subunit expression was no longer detectable on the protein or mRNA level in wild-type, Lrp4wt/ECD or Lrp4ECD/ECD muscle (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: Deleting the transmembrane and intracellular domains of LRP4 had no impact on the process of synapse elimination and AChR subunit switch at the NMJ.
source: Therefore, deleting the transmembrane and intracellular domains of LRP4 had no impact on the process of synapse elimination and AChR subunit switch (from the embryonic γ to the adult ε form) at the NMJ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing normal synapse elimination and γ-ε switch in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice.

claim: The LRP4 intracellular domain harbors no essential elements for relaying the molecular signals that govern NMJ formation.
source: These findings indicate that the LRP4 intracellular domain harbors no essential elements for relaying the molecular signals that govern NMJ formation, but that membrane anchoring of LRP4 is required for maintaining the level of signal strength necessary for postnatal growth and maturation of the neuromuscular synapses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing normal NMJ formation in Lrp4ΔICD/ΔICD mice.

claim: Membrane anchoring of LRP4 is required for maintaining the level of signal strength necessary for postnatal growth and maturation of the neuromuscular synapses.
source: These findings indicate that the LRP4 intracellular domain harbors no essential elements for relaying the molecular signals that govern NMJ formation, but that membrane anchoring of LRP4 is required for maintaining the level of signal strength necessary for postnatal growth and maturation of the neuromuscular synapses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing impaired postnatal growth in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice.

claim: Secretion of the extracellular domain of LRP4 into the pericellular space is sufficient to initiate clustering of AChRs and thus manifestation of immature NMJs.
source: On the other hand, secretion of the extracellular domain of LRP4 into the pericellular space is apparently sufficient to initiate clustering of AChRs and thus manifestation of immature NMJs that can then be maintained at the prevailing reduced signal strength.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing NMJ formation in Lrp4ECD/ECD embryos.

claim: Conditional MuSK inactivation results in NMJ disassembly in postnatal muscle.
source: This is consistent with the findings in conditional Musk knockout mice (Hesser et al., 2006), which showed NMJ disassembly in postnatal muscle upon conditional MuSK inactivation, indicating the requirement for continuous MuSK activity in postnatal muscle.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hesser et al., 2006.

claim: Continuous MuSK activity is required in postnatal muscle.
source: This is consistent with the findings in conditional Musk knockout mice (Hesser et al., 2006), which showed NMJ disassembly in postnatal muscle upon conditional MuSK inactivation, indicating the requirement for continuous MuSK activity in postnatal muscle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings in conditional Musk knockout mice and supported by citation to Hesser et al., 2006.

claim: Several ApoE receptors have been reported to interact directly or indirectly with APP.
source: However, several ApoE receptors have also been reported to interact directly or indirectly with APP (Kounnas et al., 1995; Ulery et al., 2000; Pietrzik et al., 2002; Andersen et al., 2005; Hoe et al., 2005; Pietrzik and Jaeger, 2008; Marzolo and Bu, 2009), and APP itself has been shown to participate in NMJ development (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Kounnas et al., 1995; Ulery et al., 2000; Pietrzik et al., 2002; and others.

claim: APP participates in NMJ development.
source: However, several ApoE receptors have also been reported to interact directly or indirectly with APP (Kounnas et al., 1995; Ulery et al., 2000; Pietrzik et al., 2002; Andersen et al., 2005; Hoe et al., 2005; Pietrzik and Jaeger, 2008; Marzolo and Bu, 2009), and APP itself has been shown to participate in NMJ development (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Postnatal survival of compound mutant mice was markedly reduced when three wild-type Lrp4 and App alleles were deleted.
source: We found that postnatal survival of compound mutant mice was markedly reduced when three wild-type Lrp4 and App alleles were deleted (e.g., Lrp4+/ECDApp–/– or Lrp4ECD/ECDApp+/–) and that the survival of double mutant mice (Lrp4ECD/ECDApp–/–) was significantly reduced (p<0.01) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The survival of double mutant mice (Lrp4ECD/ECDApp–/–) was significantly reduced (p<0.01).
source: We found that postnatal survival of compound mutant mice was markedly reduced when three wild-type Lrp4 and App alleles were deleted (e.g., Lrp4+/ECDApp–/– or Lrp4ECD/ECDApp+/–) and that the survival of double mutant mice (Lrp4ECD/ECDApp–/–) was significantly reduced (p<0.01) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Normal size of AChR clusters was observed at the NMJ of App–/– embryos.
source: As has been reported earlier (Wang et al., 2005), normal size of AChR clusters was observed at the NMJ of App–/– embryos (Figure 4A,B, d–f, compared to wild type in subpanels a–c, Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B,C and citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: In Lrp4ECD/ECD embryos, AChR cluster size was similar to wild-type muscles, but AChR density was decreased.
source: In Lrp4ECD/ECD embryos, AChR cluster size was similar to wild-type muscles, but AChR density was decreased (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In Lrp4ECD/ECDApp–/– double mutant embryos, both the density and the size of AChR clusters were significantly reduced compared to wild-type, App–/– or Lrp4ECD/ECD single mutant mice.
source: However, in Lrp4ECD/ECDApp–/– double mutant embryos, both the density and the size of AChR clusters were significantly reduced compared to wild-type, App–/– or Lrp4ECD/ECD single mutant mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Nerve terminal sprouting was markedly increased in the double mutant mice.
source: Furthermore, nerve terminal sprouting was markedly increased in the double mutant mice (Figure 4A,B,j–l).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Similar findings were obtained in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice lacking the amyloid precursor protein family member APLP2.
source: Similar findings were obtained in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice lacking the amyloid precursor protein family member APLP2 (Figure 5), which cooperates with APP in the development of the NMJ (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: APLP2 cooperates with APP in the development of the NMJ.
source: Similar findings were obtained in Lrp4ECD/ECD mice lacking the amyloid precursor protein family member APLP2 (Figure 5), which cooperates with APP in the development of the NMJ (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Specific, ectodomain-dependent interaction of APP and LRP4 fusion proteins occurs.
source: Figure 6A shows that specific, ectodomain-dependent interaction of both fusion proteins does indeed occur.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Significantly more and larger aggregates formed in the presence of APP and LRP4 than in control experiments.
source: Significantly more and larger aggregates formed in the presence of APP and LRP4 than in control experiments in which cells were only transfected with GFP, RFP, APP+GFP, and LRP4+RFP, respectively (Figure 6C, note approximately equal numbers of APP and LRP4 expressing cells in the aggregates in Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Homophilic interaction of APP has been reported.
source: Although homophilic interaction of APP has been reported (Soba et al., 2005), no increase in the number of large clusters was detected in wells containing only APP or LRP4 expressing cells, indicating a higher affinity of APP for LRP4 than for itself.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Soba et al., 2005.

claim: APP has a higher affinity for LRP4 than for itself.
source: Although homophilic interaction of APP has been reported (Soba et al., 2005), no increase in the number of large clusters was detected in wells containing only APP or LRP4 expressing cells, indicating a higher affinity of APP for LRP4 than for itself.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no increase in large clusters with APP or LRP4 alone.

claim: APP-Fc beads, but not RAP-Fc beads, significantly increased AChR clustering in the absence of exogenous neuronal agrin.
source: Figure 7A shows that APP-Fc beads, but not RAP-Fc beads, significantly increased AChR clustering in the absence of exogenous neuronal agrin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the presence of a low concentration of agrin (0.1 ng/ml), only APP-Fc, but not RAP-Fc, significantly increased AChR clustering.
source: When the same experiment was performed in the presence of a low concentration of agrin (0.1 ng/ml), again only APP-Fc, but not RAP-Fc, significantly increased AChR clustering.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: APP and agrin function synergistically through LRP4 to stimulate AChR clustering and NMJ formation.
source: These results indicate that APP and agrin function synergistically through LRP4 to stimulate AChR clustering and NMJ formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing synergistic effects of APP and agrin on AChR clustering.

claim: Soluble APP-Fc not bound to beads was able to promote AChR clustering.
source: Interestingly, soluble APP-Fc not bound to beads was also able to promote AChR clustering, suggesting that focal clustering of APP on opposing beads is not required, but that the interaction of APP, either in a dimeric (APP-Fc) or monomeric (APP-FLAG) form (Figure 7B), with the myotube surface is sufficient to induce initial clustering.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The interaction of APP with the myotube surface is sufficient to induce initial clustering.
source: Interestingly, soluble APP-Fc not bound to beads was also able to promote AChR clustering, suggesting that focal clustering of APP on opposing beads is not required, but that the interaction of APP, either in a dimeric (APP-Fc) or monomeric (APP-FLAG) form (Figure 7B), with the myotube surface is sufficient to induce initial clustering.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing AChR clustering with soluble APP-Fc.

claim: The soluble LRP4-ligand binding domain (MBP-LRP4) was capable of inducing clustering, alone or together with the APP-ectodomain.
source: The soluble LRP4-ligand binding domain (MBP-LRP4) was also capable of inducing clustering, alone or together with the APP-ectodomain (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The failure of RAP-Fc to induce AChR clustering suggests that LRP4 dimerization alone is not sufficient.
source: Moreover, the failure of RAP-Fc to induce AChR clustering suggests that LRP4 dimerization alone is not sufficient, but that possibly the formation of an extracellular scaffold (Bromann et al., 2004) through interactions with other surface proteins, which can be mediated by APP and LRP4 ECD, is required.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no AChR clustering with RAP-Fc and supported by citation to Bromann et al., 2004.

claim: At low concentrations (0.1 nM) agrin alone increased MuSK phosphorylation by 5.4-fold over baseline.
source: At low concentrations (0.1 nM) agrin alone increased MuSK phosphorylation by 5.4-fold over baseline.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: RAP-Fc had no effect on MuSK phosphorylation.
source: RAP-Fc was used as a control and had no effect, whereas APP-Fc alone also dose-dependently increased MuSK phosphorylation, although not as effectively as agrin (2.4, 3.2 and 4.3-fold over baseline at 1×, 10× or 100× molar concentrations, respectively, compared to 0.1 nM agrin alone).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: APP-Fc alone dose-dependently increased MuSK phosphorylation, although not as effectively as agrin.
source: RAP-Fc was used as a control and had no effect, whereas APP-Fc alone also dose-dependently increased MuSK phosphorylation, although not as effectively as agrin (2.4, 3.2 and 4.3-fold over baseline at 1×, 10× or 100× molar concentrations, respectively, compared to 0.1 nM agrin alone).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: At low (0.1 nM) to intermediate (1 nM) concentrations APP-Fc significantly increased MuSK phosphorylation by agrin further.
source: However, at low (0.1 nM) to intermediate (1 nM) concentrations APP-Fc significantly increased MuSK phosphorylation by agrin further (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: At higher concentration (10 nM), APP-Fc became less effective.
source: At higher concentration (10 nM), APP-Fc became less effective, suggesting that APP and agrin cooperatively enhance MuSK phosphorylation within a narrow physiological concentration range.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: APP and agrin cooperatively enhance MuSK phosphorylation within a narrow physiological concentration range.
source: At higher concentration (10 nM), APP-Fc became less effective, suggesting that APP and agrin cooperatively enhance MuSK phosphorylation within a narrow physiological concentration range.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing concentration-dependent effects of APP-Fc on MuSK phosphorylation.

claim: Recombinant APP-Fc failed to induce any detectable AChR clustering in LRP4 or MuSK deficient myotubes.
source: As was expected from the analysis of mice genetically deficient for LRP4 or MuSK, respectively, recombinant APP-Fc failed to induce any detectable AChR clustering in LRP4 or MuSK deficient myotubes (Figure 7E), indicating that APP can enhance but not bypass the essential activities of LRP4 and MuSK in NMJ formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: APP can enhance but not bypass the essential activities of LRP4 and MuSK in NMJ formation.
source: As was expected from the analysis of mice genetically deficient for LRP4 or MuSK, respectively, recombinant APP-Fc failed to induce any detectable AChR clustering in LRP4 or MuSK deficient myotubes (Figure 7E), indicating that APP can enhance but not bypass the essential activities of LRP4 and MuSK in NMJ formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no AChR clustering in LRP4 or MuSK deficient myotubes with APP-Fc.

claim: Only LRP4 co-precipitated with APP and with MuSK, indicating that these three proteins are already present in muscle in a preformed stable complex.
source: Remarkably, only LRP4 co-precipitated with APP and with MuSK, indicating that these three proteins are already present in muscle in a preformed stable complex (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: LRP4-Fc efficiently bound agrin at much lower concentrations than was required to achieve comparable binding to APP-Fc.
source: LRP4-Fc efficiently bound agrin at much lower concentrations than was required to achieve comparable binding to APP-Fc (Figure 8B), while RAP-Fc did not interact with agrin at all.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: RAP-Fc did not interact with agrin.
source: LRP4-Fc efficiently bound agrin at much lower concentrations than was required to achieve comparable binding to APP-Fc (Figure 8B), while RAP-Fc did not interact with agrin at all.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Agrin dose-dependently enhanced the interaction of LRP4 with APP at 10 ng/ml (1.3-fold) up to an optimal concentration ratio of 30 ng/ml (threefold higher binding than in the absence of agrin).
source: As shown in Figure 8C, agrin dose-dependently enhanced the interaction of LRP4 with APP at 10 ng/ml (1.3-fold) up to an optimal concentration ratio of 30 ng/ml (threefold higher binding than in the absence of agrin).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Higher concentrations of agrin potently inhibited the interaction of LRP4 with APP to 60% of baseline at 100 ng/ml and 10% at 300 ng/ml.
source: Higher concentrations of agrin potently inhibited the interaction of LRP4 with APP to 60% of baseline at 100 ng/ml and 10% at 300 ng/ml, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: At 1000 ng/ml agrin, which equates to an approximately 15-fold molar excess of agrin, LRP4 binding to APP was completely abolished.
source: At 1000 ng/ml, which equates to an approximately 15-fold molar excess of agrin, LRP4 binding to APP was completely abolished.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: LRP4 and APP may bind agrin through different epitopes.
source: This finding suggests that LRP4 and APP may bind agrin through different epitopes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing concentration-dependent effects of agrin on LRP4-APP interaction.

claim: All three agrin isoforms (Z0, Z8 and Z19) interact with APP.
source: Figure 8D shows that all three agrin isoforms (Z0, Z8 and Z19) interact with APP, although Z0 binding to APP appears less robust than Z8 or Z19 does.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Z0 binding to APP appears less robust than Z8 or Z19.
source: Figure 8D shows that all three agrin isoforms (Z0, Z8 and Z19) interact with APP, although Z0 binding to APP appears less robust than Z8 or Z19 does.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: AChRs clusters are prepatterned in E14.5 muscle.
source: Consistent with previous report that AChRs clusters are prepatterned in E14.5 muscle (Lin et al., 2001, Chen et al., 2011), AChR clusters were aligned along the central region of E14.5 wild-type muscle, and the majority of AChR clusters were near, but not directly apposed by presynaptic nerve terminals (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9 and citations to Lin et al., 2001, Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Prepatterned AChRs were distributed along the central region of App–/–;Aplp2–/– muscle.
source: Similarly, prepatterned AChRs were distributed along the central region of App–/–;Aplp2–/– muscle, although individual AChR clusters appear less robust compared with those in the wild-type, App–/– or Aplp2–/– muscles.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Pre-patterned AChR clustering is maintained in the absence of APP and APLP2.
source: These results demonstrate that pre-patterned AChR clustering is maintained in the absence of APP and APLP2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing prepatterned AChRs in App–/–;Aplp2–/– muscle.

claim: LRP4 staining was clearly visible at the NMJ in E18.5 WT muscle.
source: By contrast, specific LRP4 staining was clearly visible at the NMJ in E18.5 WT muscle (Figure 10A,h), although the staining was markedly weaker at earlier developmental stages (E14.5 [Figure 10A,b] and E16.5 [Figure 10A,e]).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: APP was localized at the NMJ in E18.5 WT muscle.
source: Similarly, APP was also localized at the NMJ in E18.5 WT muscle (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: LRP4 staining was detected at the NMJ in Lrp4ECD/ECD muscle, but at reduced levels compared with WT muscle.
source: In Lrp4ECD/ECD muscle (Figure 10C,e), we detected LRP4 staining at the NMJ, but at reduced levels compared with WT muscle (Figure 10D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10C,D.

claim: LRP4 staining was reduced in App–/–;Aplp2–/– double mutant muscle, compared to WT muscle.
source: Strikingly, LRP4 staining was also reduced in App–/–;Aplp2–/– double mutant muscle (Figure 10C,h), compared to WT muscle (Figure 10D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10C,D.

claim: Higher LRP4 protein expression was detected in Lrp4ECD/ECD compared to WT muscle in adult muscle (hindlimb, 10-week-old).
source: In adult muscle (hindlimb, 10-week-old), higher LRP4 protein (Figure 10E) and mRNA (Figure 10F) expression were detected in Lrp4ECD/ECD compared to WT muscle.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10E,F.

claim: Higher LRP4 mRNA expression was detected in Lrp4ECD/ECD compared to WT muscle in adult muscle (hindlimb, 10-week-old).
source: In adult muscle (hindlimb, 10-week-old), higher LRP4 protein (Figure 10E) and mRNA (Figure 10F) expression were detected in Lrp4ECD/ECD compared to WT muscle.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10E,F.

claim: APP interacts directly with LRP4.
source: Our results have revealed previously unrecognized interactions at the NMJ between LRP4 and APP on the one hand and APP and agrin on the other.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: APP interacts directly with agrin.
source: Our results have revealed previously unrecognized interactions at the NMJ between LRP4 and APP on the one hand and APP and agrin on the other.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: LRP4 and APP functionally interact to regulate NMJ development and maintenance.
source: Genetic epistasis experiments show that LRP4 and APP functionally interact to regulate NMJ development and maintenance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: APP is capable of activating MuSK (at a low level and independent of agrin) by ligating and clustering LRP4.
source: APP may accomplish this through several independent mechanisms: first, APP interacts directly with LRP4 and thereby is capable of activating MuSK (at a low level and independent of agrin) by ligating and clustering LRP4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Agrin cooperatively increases the stoichiometric interaction of APP with LRP4.
source: Second, APP can also directly bind to agrin, albeit at lower affinity than LRP4. However, agrin cooperatively increases the stoichiometric interaction of APP with LRP4, which may serve to focus MuSK activation and thereby prevent aberrant AChR clustering.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: APP and its homologues bind homomerically and heteromerically to each other.
source: Third, APP and its homologues, which are expressed pre- and post-synaptically (Wang et al., 2005), bind homomerically and heteromerically to each other (Soba et al., 2005), thereby generating or strengthening attachment sites for nerve terminals (Torroja et al., 1999; Akaaboune et al., 2000; Soba et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Soba et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005.

claim: APP and its homologues generate or strengthen attachment sites for nerve terminals.
source: Third, APP and its homologues, which are expressed pre- and post-synaptically (Wang et al., 2005), bind homomerically and heteromerically to each other (Soba et al., 2005), thereby generating or strengthening attachment sites for nerve terminals (Torroja et al., 1999; Akaaboune et al., 2000; Soba et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Torroja et al., 1999; Akaaboune et al., 2000; Soba et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Initial AChR clustering is independent of neuronal agrin.
source: Also supporting this model is the finding that initial AChR clustering is independent of neuronal agrin (Lin et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001) and that rudimentary NMJs form in agrin-deficient mice (Gautam et al., 1996), which suggested the existence of a second nerve derived organizing signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001.

claim: Rudimentary NMJs form in agrin-deficient mice.
source: Also supporting this model is the finding that initial AChR clustering is independent of neuronal agrin (Lin et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001) and that rudimentary NMJs form in agrin-deficient mice (Gautam et al., 1996), which suggested the existence of a second nerve derived organizing signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gautam et al., 1996.

claim: NMJs completely fail to form in Musk knockout mice.
source: By contrast, NMJs completely fail to form in Musk (DeChiara et al., 1996) and Lrp4 (Weatherbee et al., 2006) knockout mice, indicating an absolute requirement for MuSK and LRP4.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to DeChiara et al., 1996.

claim: NMJs completely fail to form in Lrp4 knockout mice.
source: By contrast, NMJs completely fail to form in Musk (DeChiara et al., 1996) and Lrp4 (Weatherbee et al., 2006) knockout mice, indicating an absolute requirement for MuSK and LRP4.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weatherbee et al., 2006.

claim: The intracellular domain of APP appears to be required for normal NMJ development.
source: Interestingly, however, and in contrast to our results with LRP4, the intracellular domain of APP appears to be required for normal NMJ development (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2010.

claim: Immobilized, but not soluble, agrin is able to aggregate MuSK and promote AChR clustering independent of MuSK's kinase activity.
source: In their study, Bromann and colleagues further showed that immobilized, but not soluble, agrin is able to aggregate MuSK and promote AChR clustering independent of MuSK's kinase activity, suggesting that MuSK scaffolding plays an important role in AChR clustering.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bromann et al., 2004.

claim: MuSK scaffolding plays an important role in AChR clustering.
source: In their study, Bromann and colleagues further showed that immobilized, but not soluble, agrin is able to aggregate MuSK and promote AChR clustering independent of MuSK's kinase activity, suggesting that MuSK scaffolding plays an important role in AChR clustering.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings of Bromann et al., 2004.

claim: AChR clustering can be mediated by treatment with neuraminidase and VVA lectin.
source: AChR clustering can also be mediated by a variety of agrin independent mechanisms, including treatment with neuraminidase and VVA lectin (Martin and Sanes, 1995; Grow et al., 1999a,b) and by defucosylation of muscle agrin, which unmask its ability to induce MuSK phosphorylation (Kim et al., 2008a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martin and Sanes, 1995; Grow et al., 1999a,b.

claim: Defucosylation of muscle agrin unmasks its ability to induce MuSK phosphorylation.
source: AChR clustering can also be mediated by a variety of agrin independent mechanisms, including treatment with neuraminidase and VVA lectin (Martin and Sanes, 1995; Grow et al., 1999a,b) and by defucosylation of muscle agrin, which unmask its ability to induce MuSK phosphorylation (Kim et al., 2008a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2008a.

claim: Mice lacking both App family members exhibit aberrant apposition of presynaptic marker proteins with postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors and excessive nerve terminal sprouting and a reduced number of synaptic vesicles at presynaptic terminals.
source: Like App, Aplp2 is also required for normal NMJ formation, and mice lacking both App family members exhibit aberrant apposition of presynaptic marker proteins with postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors and excessive nerve terminal sprouting and a reduced number of synaptic vesicles at presynaptic terminals (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Functional NMJ formation is significantly compromised in the Lrp4ECD/ECD;Aplp2–/– double mutants.
source: However, as in Lrp4ECD/ECD;App−/−, functional NMJ formation, as evidenced by greatly impaired postnatal survival (Table 2) and AChR clustering (Figure 5), is also significantly compromised in the Lrp4ECD/ECD;Aplp2–/– double mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2 and Figure 5.

claim: LRP4 can interact with several modulators of the Wnt pathways, that is Wise, Dkk, and Sost.
source: On another note, we have previously shown that LRP4 can interact with several modulators of the Wnt pathways, that is Wise, Dkk, and Sost (Dietrich et al., 2010; Karner et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dietrich et al., 2010; Karner et al., 2010.

claim: ApoE in an AD-associated, isoform-specific manner impairs ApoE receptor recycling at central synapses.
source: We have recently shown that ApoE in an AD-associated, isoform-specific manner impairs ApoE receptor recycling at central synapses (Chen et al., 2010b) and that this impairs the ability of ApoE receptor-dependent signals to prevent β-amyloid induced synaptic suppression (Durakoglugil et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2010b.

claim: Impaired ApoE receptor recycling impairs the ability of ApoE receptor-dependent signals to prevent β-amyloid induced synaptic suppression.
source: We have recently shown that ApoE in an AD-associated, isoform-specific manner impairs ApoE receptor recycling at central synapses (Chen et al., 2010b) and that this impairs the ability of ApoE receptor-dependent signals to prevent β-amyloid induced synaptic suppression (Durakoglugil et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Durakoglugil et al., 2009.

claim: Perturbed APP synaptic adhesion activity may contribute to synaptic dysfunction and AD pathogenesis.
source: The findings we have reported here, together with those by Wang et al., who have proposed that perturbed APP synaptic adhesion activity may contribute to synaptic dysfunction and AD pathogenesis (Wang et al., 2009), reaffirm the NMJ as a versatile and useful experimental model system on which the cell biology of ApoE, APP and ApoE receptor trafficking and its pathobiology at peripheral and central synapses can be investigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2009.
